name: Millerism
notes: William Miller first publicly taught his second advent expectation in 1831.
summary: An interdenominational Advent revival organized around William Miller’s expectation of Christ’s near return.
formation_narrative: Miller’s reading of Daniel led him to expect a literal return of Christ in the 1840s. Public lectures, Himes’s publishing work, and camp meetings carried the message across denominational lines. The failed expectations of 1844 produced deep disappointment and competing explanations. Some followers abandoned the movement; others reorganized into distinct Adventist traditions. It was a revival network rather than a single church that formally dissolved on one date.
core_beliefs: Prophetic expectation: Daniel’s time periods were read as pointing toward an imminent, visible advent.
Evangelistic urgency: hearers were urged to repent and prepare rather than assume ordinary history would continue indefinitely.
Divergent aftermath: later Sabbath, sanctuary, and mortality teachings cannot all be assigned to Miller’s original coalition.

profile_scope: This is an introductory profile. It distinguishes shared teaching from historical development; sources do not imply that every member held an identical position. No formal corporate dissolution is asserted for this historical process. The status is unknown at the institutional level; the ending narrative explains its diffusion or development.
ending_narrative: The failure of the 1844 expectations broke the revival’s shared momentum and led to competing explanations and organizations. It did not end through a single legal dissolution. Later Adventist churches preserved different portions of the inheritance; they are multiple descendants rather than parties to one universal terminal merger.

name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
summary: A global Adventist denomination joining expectation of Christ’s return with seventh-day Sabbath observance and a developed theology of Christ’s ministry.
formation_narrative: Sabbatarian believers emerging from the Millerite disappointment gradually developed a common identity, publications, and organization. The General Conference was organized in Battle Creek in May 1863. The resulting denomination combined mission, education, and health work with distinctive interpretation of the Sabbath and heavenly sanctuary. Its current beliefs reflect development beyond the original Millerite coalition, not an unchanged creed carried intact from 1844.
core_beliefs: Sabbath: Saturday is observed as a biblical day of worship and rest.
Christ and judgment: the church teaches Christ’s return and an ongoing heavenly ministry, including a pre-advent judgment associated with 1844.

Scripture and discipleship: the 28 Fundamental Beliefs explain its reading of Scripture, including baptism, resurrection, spiritual gifts, and care for health; Ellen White’s prophetic ministry is affirmed within this framework.

name: Advent Christian Church
summary: An Adventist communion emphasizing Christ’s return, resurrection, and immortality as God’s gift rather than an inherent human possession.
formation_narrative: Advent Christians developed within the post-Millerite search for a sustainable Advent witness, organizing in the nineteenth century rather than adopting the Sabbatarian Adventist system. The existing 1860 date marks organizational origins. Their identity joins evangelical faith with conditional immortality and the expectation of Christ’s return. Contemporary statements must be checked for adoption status: the proposed 2026 Declaration of Principles did not receive the required vote.
core_beliefs: Conditional immortality: eternal life is given through Christ; the unsaved are not understood as possessing an inherently immortal soul.
Advent hope: resurrection and Christ’s future return are central to the church’s message.
Christian worship and liberty: the published Declaration describes first-day worship and allows conscience on matters such as military service. It should not be confused with seventh-day Adventism.

key_documents.significance: Published denominational principles explaining Adventist distinctives; consult the adopted text rather than treating the proposed 2026 revision as operative.

profile_scope: Individual founder attribution and the detailed 1860 organizational proceedings still need deeper archival research; the 2026 adoption outcome is directly documented.
ending_narrative: The Advent Christian communion continues. Debate over principles remains part of its development: the proposed 2026 declaration did not achieve the required adoption vote, which did not itself dissolve the church or create a successor denomination.

name: Church of God (Seventh Day)
notes: Sabbatarian Adventist line separating in 1858 before the SDA organization.
summary: A Sabbath-observing Adventist denomination whose identity centers on Christ, biblical authority, and resurrection hope.
formation_narrative: The church traces its development to believers in western Michigan in 1858. It grew within the Sabbatarian Adventist environment while developing separately from the denomination that became Seventh-day Adventist. Publishing and later conference organization sustained the fellowship. This node refers principally to the General Conference tradition; similarly named Church of God bodies are not automatically the same organization.
core_beliefs: Seventh-day Sabbath: Saturday observance expresses gratitude and rest in God, rather than earning salvation.
Grace and ordinances: salvation is through Christ; believer’s baptism and the Lord’s Supper visibly express faith.
Resurrection hope and Scripture: Scripture governs teaching, and final life depends on God’s resurrection and judgment rather than natural human immortality.

key_documents.significance: The General Conference’s published doctrinal summary; its scope should not be extended to every unrelated Church of God organization.

profile_scope: This is an introductory profile. It distinguishes shared teaching from historical development; sources do not imply that every member held an identical position.
ending_narrative: The fellowship developed from early congregations and publishing into a General Conference organized in 1884 and incorporated in 1899. It continues today with autonomous national sister conferences. These are stages of organization and cooperation, not evidence of a terminal merger into Seventh-day Adventism.
